text: At a shaadi the dhol starts, the lights flash, everyone is delighted, and you're quietly counting the minutes until you can stand outside for a while.
Someone asks why you're so quiet, and the whole room turns to wait for your answer.
You can't eat something because of its texture, and somebody calls it nakhray. Again.
You spend all of Eid, or a wedding, or a family visit being ‘normal’, then need the whole next day in a dark room to recover.
You finally find the words to explain, and someone says ‘sab ke saath hota hai’, it happens to everyone.
The conversation about your future turns to whether you're ‘a bit different’, and everyone nods as if that settles something.
Every report card said some version of ‘intelligent, but careless’.
You understood the lesson perfectly, then lost all of it the moment you had to copy it off the board.
You read the same paragraph four times and it still won't stay.
You were the ‘naughty one’ in class for not being able to sit still, and after a while you believed it.
You rehearse a phone call three times before you dial, then apologise for taking up their time.
The fan clicking, someone's ringtone, the smell of lunch, three conversations at once. You get nothing done, and it looks like laziness.
The tube light is buzzing and nobody else seems to hear it.
A hug you didn't expect feels like too much, and then you feel guilty for flinching.
There's a seam or a label somewhere in your clothes, and it's all you can think about.
Horns, traffic, a crowded bazaar. By the time you get home there's nothing left of you for anyone.
Your mind has twelve tabs open, and the one thing that matters is the one you can't make yourself start.
You love something with your whole heart, and someone calls you ‘obsessed’ as if it's a problem.
You're still replaying a conversation from last week, trying to work out if you said it wrong.
When you're focused you forget to eat. When you're not, you forget why you walked into the kitchen.
Everyone else seems to have a rulebook for talking to people, and nobody ever gave you a copy.
You've been told it's laziness, too much phone, bad upbringing or nazar. Nobody asked what it's actually like for you.
You mention a diagnosis and someone says, ‘But you don't look like it.’
You've only ever read about this in English, about people in other countries, and wondered whether it counts for you too.
You don't have a diagnosis. You're still wondering, and you're not sure you're allowed to relate. You are.
